Solo Motorcycle Touring: Safe and Self-Sufficient

Solo motorcycle touring is a profoundly rewarding experience. No compromises on route or pace, no waiting for slower riders, and a connection with the road and landscape that group riding simply can't match. But riding alone in remote areas requires extra preparation and awareness. Here's how to do it safely.

Tell Someone Your Plans

The single most important safety measure for solo touring is making sure someone knows where you are:

  • Share your daily route and overnight stops with a trusted contact
  • Use a shared Google Doc or Live Location sharing on WhatsApp
  • Check in by text at the end of each day
  • Agree a protocol — if they haven't heard from you by a certain time, they should try to reach you and escalate if needed

Self-Sufficiency Kit

When you're alone, there's no one to ride for help. Carry more than you would in a group:

  • Comprehensive first aid kit: Include trauma dressings, triangular bandages, and antiseptic — not just plasters.
  • Full tool roll: Enough to handle common roadside repairs.
  • Tyre repair kit and compressor: A puncture when solo is a bigger problem than in a group. Be able to fix it yourself.
  • Emergency bivvy bag: Weighs 100g, could save your life if you're stranded overnight.
  • Water and snacks: Always carry at least 500ml of water and energy food.
  • Torch (head torch): If you're stuck after dark, you need hands-free light.

Emergency Communication

In areas without phone signal — and there are many in touring Britain — you need backup options:

  • What3Words app: Downloaded with offline functionality, it gives emergency services your exact location using three words.
  • Personal Locator Beacon (PLB): A PLB works via satellite regardless of phone signal. Press the button and coastguard/mountain rescue will find you. Costs £200-300 but could be the best investment you make.
  • Satellite communicator: Devices like the Garmin inReach allow two-way satellite messaging and SOS from anywhere. Monthly subscription required.
Solo touring isn't riskier than group touring if you prepare properly. The main difference is that you're your own safety net. Pack for self-sufficiency, communicate your plans, and trust your judgement.

Riding Approach When Solo

Your riding style should be slightly more conservative when alone:

  • Ride at 80% of your comfortable limit. There's no one to impress and no one to help if you push too hard.
  • Take more rest breaks. Without the social stimulus of group riding, fatigue can sneak up more easily.
  • Be extra cautious in wet conditions and on unfamiliar roads.
  • Never ride when you're tired, cold, or hungry. As a solo tourer, your judgement is your most important safety tool.

Accommodation Safety

  • When wild camping solo, choose discreet locations away from roads
  • Lock your bike securely at night, wherever you're sleeping
  • Let your contact know where you're camping for the night
  • Trust your instincts — if a location feels wrong, move on

The Social Side of Solo Touring

Riding solo doesn't mean being alone all the time. Some of the best connections happen because you're on your own:

  • Other bikers will chat to you at fuel stops and viewpoints
  • B&B hosts and pub locals are more likely to engage with a solo traveller
  • You'll meet people at campsites who share your passion
  • Biker cafes are social hubs where solo riders are always welcome

Solo motorcycle touring is freedom in its purest form. Prepare well, ride sensibly, and embrace the solitude — some of your finest memories on two wheels will come from these solo miles.

faq.a: Solo touring is not inherently riskier than group riding if you prepare properly. The key difference is that you are your own safety net, so you must pack for self-sufficiency, communicate your plans and ride more conservatively. Tell someone your route, carry a way to summon help without phone signal, and ride at around 80% of your limit.

faq.q: How do I call for help where there is no phone signal?
faq.a: Large parts of touring Britain, including the Highlands and mid-Wales, have no mobile coverage. Download the What3Words app for offline location referencing, and for genuine remote riding consider a Personal Locator Beacon or a satellite communicator such as a Garmin inReach, both of which work via satellite regardless of phone signal.

faq.q: What extra kit should a solo rider carry?
faq.a: Beyond normal touring gear, carry a comprehensive first aid kit with trauma dressings, a full tool roll, a tyre repair kit with compressor, an emergency bivvy bag, at least 500ml of water and energy food, and a head torch. When alone there is nobody to fetch help, so you need to handle common roadside problems yourself.

faq.q: Is it safe to wild camp alone?
faq.a: Yes, with sensible precautions. Choose discreet spots away from roads, lock your bike securely, and let your contact know exactly where you are camping. Trust your instincts: if a location feels wrong, move on. In genuinely remote areas your bike is unlikely to be disturbed, but a disc lock and cover help you sleep easier.
